headline: Approved variances for a garage-to-home conversion at 5 Morgan Street and a drive-through restaurant at 427-429 Amherst Street.
summary: The applicant withdrew a plan for five duplex buildings at 3 Ayer Road. The panel approved, 4-1, converting a garage at 5 Morgan Street into a single-family home. A setback variance for a drive-through restaurant at 427-429 and 431 Amherst Street was approved 5-0.
decisions: Withdrawn by the applicant: plan for five duplex buildings at 3 Ayer Road.
Approved variances to convert a garage at 5 Morgan Street into a single-family home, 4-1.
Approved a variance for a drive-through restaurant's distance from residential land at 427-429 and 431 Amherst Street, 5-0.

EXPANDED DRAFT MEETING SUMMARY  
THIS IS NOT AN OFFICIAL TRANSCRIPT OF TAPE-RECORDED PROCEEDINGS THE INFORMATION 
CONTAINED HEREIN HAS NOT BEEN REVIEWED OR APPROVED BY THE ZBA 
ZONING BOARD OF ADJUSTMENT PUBLIC HEARING AND MEETING 
Tuesday, November 10, 2026 
A public hearing of the Zoning Board of Adjustment was held on 
Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at 6:30 PM, in the 3rd floor 
auditorium at Nashua City Hall, 229 Main Street, Nashua, NH. 
Jay Minkarah, Chair, asked for a Roll Call:  
Jay Minkarah, Chair  
Josh Nehiley, Vice Chair  
JP Boucher, Member Steve Lionel, Member  
Joseph Patry, Member  
 
Sam Durfee, Planning Manager 
Mr. Minkarah welcomed the public and noted that all five members 
were present, constituting a full board. 
Mr. Minkarah explained the ZBA procedures, stating that the 
public is invited to present cases within a fifteen-minute 
timeframe. He noted that comments could be submitted for future 
meetings via email to zb@nashuanh.gov or by mail to P.O. Box 
2019, Nashua, NH. He identified the points of law required for 
applicants to address relative to variances, explaining that an 
applicant must satisfy five specific statutory criteria: that 
the variance will not be contrary to the public interest, the 
spirit of the ordinance is observed, substantial justice is 
done, surrounding property values are not diminished, and 
literal enforcement would result in an unnecessary hardship due 
to special conditions of the property. He outlined the order of 
testimony, providing applicants up to 15 minutes for 
presentation, followed by 5-minute periods for speakers in 
favor, speakers in opposition or with questions, a 5-minute 
rebuttal for the applicant, and a final 5-minute closing for a 
designated opposition spokesperson. 
Mr. Minkarah announced that the following case was withdrawn as 
reflected in the amended agenda: Case No. 3: Ayer Rd, LLC 
(Owner) 3 Ayer Road (Sheet G Lot 12) requesting the following: 
1) Use variance from Land Use Code Section 190-15, Table 15-1 
(#6), to allow five duplex residential buildings in the R18 
Zone, 2) from Land Use Code Section 190-17 (B), to allow more 
than one principal structure per lot, 1 permitted – 5 duplex 
buildings proposed; and, 3) from Land Use Code Section 190-16,
2 
 
Table 16-3, for minimum land area, 65,925 sq. ft exists – 
174,240 sq. ft required – all requests to remove all dilapidated 
buildings and vehicles and redevelop the lot with five duplex 
residential buildings and associated site improvements. R18 
Zone, Ward 2. [WITHDRAWN BY APPLICANT] 
 
1. Daniel J. Maffee and Karen C. Maffee, Trustees (Owner & 
Applicant) 5 Morgan Street (Sheet 42 Lot 149) requesting the 
following variances: 1) from Land Use Code Section 190-16, Table 
16-3 for minimum land area, 9,395 sq. ft. existing – 10,455 sq. 
ft. required for 3 dwellings, and 2) from Land Use Code Section 
190-17, B for more than 1 principal structure on a lot – 2 
proposed. RC Zone, Ward 3. 
Voting on this case:  
 
Jay Minkarah  
Josh Nehiley  
JP Boucher  
Steve Lionel  
Joseph Patry 
Attorney Brad Westgate, Welts, White & Fontaine, P.C., 29 
Factory Street, Nashua, NH, representing applicants Daniel J. 
Maffee and Karen C. Maffee, Trustees, presented the case. Owner 
Daniel Maffee and Ethan Beals of IMEC (plan preparer) were also 
present. 
Attorney Westgate distributed large-scale site plans and an 
annotated GIS neighborhood density map displaying unit counts 
per parcel from city assessing records, alongside two letters of 
support from neighboring property owners. He explained that the 
subject property is a 0.22-acre (9,395 square feet) L-shaped lot 
located in the RC district, currently containing an existing 
two-family dwelling (duplex), a detached garage in the rear 
setback, and paved parking areas. The lot features 60 feet of 
frontage along Morgan Street, complying with the RC district 
frontage requirement of 50 feet. 
Attorney Westgate stated that the applicants propose to convert 
the existing detached rear garage (measuring 22 feet by 50 feet, 
with an approximate 1,100-square-foot footprint) into a one-
story, single-family residential dwelling that may retain a 
smaller garage component within its existing footprint. Because 
the existing duplex will remain, two variances are required:
3 
 
first, from Section 190-17(B) to permit two principal 
residential structures on a single lot; and second, from Section 
190-16, Table 16-3 for lot area density. In the RC district, the 
density standard of 12.5 units per acre establishes a lot area 
requirement of 10,455 square feet for three dwelling units. The 
subject lot contains 9,395 square feet, representing 
approximately 90% of the required land area. He noted that the 
site complies with all other conventional dimensional standards, 
including the 35% minimum open space ratio. 
Attorney Westgate highlighted the surrounding neighborhood 
density context using the GIS map, noting that 4 Morgan Street 
contains seven units with a large rear parking lot, 2 Morgan 
Street contains four units on a significantly smaller lot, and 
25 Chandler Street is the multi-unit redevelopment of the former 
St. Francis Xavier elementary school. He reported that when 
Morgan Street was repaved earlier in the year, Mr. Maffee 
stubbed municipal water and sewer lines and extended a gas line 
to the garage at his own expense and risk to avoid cutting into 
the newly paved roadway, which is subject to a five-year 
pavement cut moratorium. He confirmed that Planning Manager Sam 
Durfee issued an administrative determination verifying the 
garage as a pre-existing non-conforming structure and 
establishing the need for the requested variances. 
SPEAKING IN FAVOR: No one spoke in person. 
Mr. Minkarah read two letters of support into the record: 
Louis Antonetti, 3 Morgan Street, Nashua, NH. Mr. Antonetti, a 
direct abutter, submitted a letter stating he is familiar with 
the property and strongly supports converting the existing 
garage into a single-family dwelling. He stated that the project 
makes productive use of an existing structure, adds needed 
housing within Nashua, complements surrounding properties, and 
represents a positive investment in the neighborhood. 
Stacy and Samuel Kirby, 63 Tolles Street, Nashua, NH. Mr. and 
Mrs. Kirby, adjacent property owners, submitted a letter stating 
they have no objection to repurposing the garage into a single 
residential dwelling and fully support the owners moving forward 
with their plans. 
SPEAKING IN OPPOSITION OR WITH QUESTIONS OR CONCERNS: No one. 
END OF PUBLIC HEARING, BEGINNING OF PUBLIC MEETING: Mr. Nehiley 
spoke in favor of the application, noting that the lot is only
4 
 
10% short of the required land area for three units. He stated 
that the GIS density extract demonstrated that the surrounding 
neighborhood contains numerous multi-unit properties on smaller 
parcels. He observed that the garage is situated squarely 
relative to neighboring structures, no letters of opposition 
were received, and the garage is functionally obsolete for 
parking modern vehicles due to the narrow driveway curve. He 
added that converting obsolete accessory buildings into viable 
housing is consistent with recent Board approvals. 
Mr. Lionel expressed difficulty with granting relief to allow 
two principal structures on a single lot, recalling previous 
applications (such as Granite Street) where the Board denied 
requests to convert accessory garages into separate single-
family dwellings. He acknowledged that the garage is 
functionally obsolete and that neighboring abutters expressed 
support, but stated he remained uncomfortable with establishing 
two principal dwellings on a single residential lot. 
Mr. Minkarah spoke in support of the application, noting that 
from a density perspective, three units on the 9,395-square-foot 
lot represents a lower density than many surrounding multi-
family properties. He highlighted the unusual L-shaped lot 
geometry and the fact that the existing garage is tucked into 
the far rear corner of the parcel. He agreed that the garage is 
an obsolete structure and emphasized that the most directly 
impacted immediate abutter at 3 Morgan Street submitted a letter 
of strong support. 
MOTION by Mr. Nehiley to approve the variance applications on 
behalf of Daniel J. Maffee and Karen C. Maffee, Trustees. 
Mr. Nehiley stated that granting the variances would not be 
contrary to the public interest because there is an existing 
structure in place and the property is situated within a densely 
packed residential neighborhood. 
Mr. Nehiley stated that the spirit of the ordinance would be 
observed because several properties in the immediate area are 
non-conforming relative to required square footage for their 
unit counts, making the proposed three-unit density consistent 
with the established character of the neighborhood. 
Mr. Nehiley stated that granting the variances would do 
substantial justice because the applicant is unable to properly 
utilize the existing obsolete garage building, expended personal 
funds to stub in municipal utilities during street repaving in a
5 
 
timely manner, and denying the request would cause a material 
adverse loss to the owner with no corresponding gain to the 
public. 
Mr. Nehiley stated that surrounding property values would not be 
diminished, as supported by letters of favor from multiple 
neighboring property owners expressing support for the property 
investment. 
Mr. Nehiley stated that owing to special conditions of the 
property, denial of the variance would result in unnecessary 
hardship because the parcel possesses a unique L-shaped geometry 
featuring an existing garage that is functionally obsolete for 
modern vehicle parking. Converting the garage within its exact 
existing footprint ensures no visual change to surrounding 
neighbors, and the property is already non-conforming due to the 
obsolete structure. 
SECONDED by Mr. Boucher.  
MOTION TO APPROVE CARRIED 4-1. Mr. Lionel in opposition. 
 
2. Stonefield Engineering and Design (Applicant) Shiv Shrestha 
(Owner) 427-429 & 431 Amherst Street (Sheet H Lots 157 & 40) 
requesting variance from Land Use Code Section 190-41, C.1 for 
minimum distance from a drive-through lane to any residential 
zoning district, 10.6 feet proposed – 30 feet required. GB & RC 
Zones, Ward 2. 
Voting on this case:  
Jay Minkarah  
Josh Nehiley  
JP Boucher  
Steve Lionel  
Joseph Patry 
Giovanni Caesar, Stonefield Engineering and Design, 120 
Washington Street, Suite 201, Salem, MA, representing applicant 
Stonefield Engineering and Design and owner Shiv Shrestha, 
presented the case. Mr. Caesar explained that the subject 
property (427-429 and 431 Amherst Street) is an active 
commercial shopping plaza hosting mixed retail and second-floor 
office uses, alongside an existing vacant commercial building at 
431 Amherst Street that historically operated as a boutique shop 
and pet groomer. The applicant proposes to raze the vacant
6 
 
building and construct a new quick-serve regional chicken 
restaurant featuring a single drive-through lane and a parallel 
bypass lane. 
Mr. Caesar stated that a variance is requested from Land Use 
Code Section 190-41(C)(1), which mandates a minimum 30-foot 
separation distance between a drive-through lane and any 
residential zoning district. The proposed plan establishes a 
10.6-foot setback from the outer edge of the bypass lane (and a 
20.6-foot setback from the drive-through lane itself) to the 
internal split-zone boundary line at the rear of the lot. He 
explained that the parcel is split-zoned, with the front 
commercial development situated in the General Business (GB) 
district and a massive, undeveloped wooded hillside at the rear 
situated in the Residence C (RC) district. 
Mr. Caesar detailed the extreme site topography, explaining that 
there is a 6-foot grade change across the commercial pad from 
Amherst Street, and a steep 48-foot elevation rise from the rear 
of the shopping center up to the residential district boundary 
near the Boulder Park Apartments on Kessler Farm Drive, creating 
a combined 56-foot elevation change. He stated that the project 
includes major site infrastructure improvements: closing one 
redundant driveway cut onto Amherst Street, installing new 
concrete sidewalks, upgrading ADA parking spaces to federal and 
state codes, and replacing failing catch basins to capture and 
treat 100% of stormwater runoff that currently flows unmanaged 
onto Amherst Street. He added that the drive-through stacking 
queue accommodates eight vehicles (160 feet), satisfying 
industry standards for a regional quick-serve user. 
SPEAKING IN FAVOR: No one. 
SPEAKING IN OPPOSITION OR WITH QUESTIONS OR CONCERNS: No one. 
END OF PUBLIC HEARING, BEGINNING OF PUBLIC MEETING: Mr. Lionel 
expressed concern regarding internal vehicle circulation and 
parking availability for existing plaza businesses, specifically 
noting that patrons of Cucina Toscana restaurant currently park 
in the area proposed for the drive-through lane. He observed 
that vehicles accessing the drive-through will pass parked cars 
along the main plaza aisle, though he acknowledged that 
circulation and parking details are under the jurisdiction of 
the Planning Board during site plan review. 
Mr. Nehiley spoke in favor of the application, noting that the 
existing vacant building is multi-level, non-ADA compliant, and
7 
 
functionally obsolete. He stated that razing the blighted 
building is a substantial benefit to Amherst Street, and that 
the engineering team has incorporated directional flow arrows 
and driveway consolidations to mitigate traffic. He expressed 
confidence that the Planning Board will thoroughly address 
internal site circulation. 
Mr. Patry spoke in favor, agreeing that the vacant building is 
obsolete and must be removed. He stated that any new commercial 
development on the pad will generate traffic, and the proposed 
redevelopment is reasonable for the commercial corridor. 
Mr. Minkarah spoke in support, stating that the primary driver 
for the variance is the technical split-zone line running 
through the commercial property. He emphasized that the intent 
of the separation rule is to protect residential occupants from 
noise and headlights. Given the steep 48-foot elevation rise and 
dense woodland buffer separating the drive-through lane from the 
elevated Boulder Park Apartments, he concluded that full 
physical protection exists. 
MOTION by Mr. Nehiley to approve the variance application on 
behalf of Stonefield Engineering and Design. 
Mr. Nehiley stated that granting the variance would not be 
contrary to the public interest because the separation 
requirement is intended to keep drive-through lanes away from 
residential dwellings, Amherst Street is an established 
commercial highway corridor, and the public interest is served 
by replacing a blighted, obsolete building. 
Mr. Nehiley stated that the spirit of the ordinance would be 
observed because the oversized parcel features a 48-foot steep 
elevation rise and dense tree buffer separating the commercial 
drive-through from the Boulder Park Apartments, ensuring that 
neighboring residential occupants are completely unaffected. 
Mr. Nehiley stated that granting the variance would do 
substantial justice because it allows the property owner to 
replace a functionally obsolete building with a modern, 
functional commercial building for an active tenant along a 
major commercial corridor. 
Mr. Nehiley stated that surrounding property values would not be 
diminished, as the project revitalizes an unlit, vacant portion 
of the commercial plaza with new lighting, modern building 
design, and engineered stormwater management infrastructure.
8 
 
Mr. Nehiley stated that owing to special conditions of the 
property, denial of the variance would result in unnecessary 
hardship because the parcel is split-zoned and possesses a 
dramatic 48-foot elevation rise directly behind the commercial 
pad, creating a unique physical constraint. There is no fair and 
substantial relationship between the literal 30-foot separation 
requirement and its specific application to this elevated, 
split-zoned site, and constructing a drive-through restaurant 
along Amherst Street is a reasonable commercial use. 
SECONDED by Mr. Patry.  
MOTION TO APPROVE CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY 5-0. 
 
MISCELLANEOUS: 
REGIONAL IMPACT: Given the November 24th meeting has been 
canceled, the Board had no cases to review for regional impact. 
MINUTES: The Board reviewed the draft minutes for the October 
27, 2026 public hearing and meeting. 
MOTION by Mr. Patry to approve the minutes of October 27, 2026 
as presented, waive the reading, and place the minutes in the 
file.  
SECONDED by Mr.  
Lionel. MOTION CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY 5-0. 
OTHER BUSINESS: 
First Reading of Board Bylaw Amendments (Postponements and 
Continuances): Planning Manager Sam Durfee presented the first 
reading of proposed amendments to Section 10 and Subsection O. 
of the Board Bylaws regarding applicant requests for hearing 
postponements or continuances: 
1. Newspaper Notice Requirement: Removal of the outdated 
requirement to publish postponement notices in the 
newspaper six days prior to a hearing, as newspaper 
publication is no longer statutorily required and Nashua no 
longer has a daily print newspaper. 
2. Two-Tiered Postponement Process: Initial written 
postponement requests submitted to staff at least six 
calendar days prior to a scheduled public hearing (prior to 
12:00 PM noon) may be granted administratively by staff.
9 
 
Any postponement request submitted within six calendar days 
of a hearing, or any second or subsequent postponement 
request for a case, must be formally presented to and voted 
on by the ZBA at the public hearing. 
3. Process: Formally noticed on the agenda as the first 
reading. A second reading and final vote for adoption will 
occur at the December 8, 2026 meeting. 
ADJOURNMENT: MOTION by Mr. Lionel to adjourn the meeting at 7:19 
PM. SECONDED by Mr. Patry. MOTION CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY. 
Submitted by: Sam Durfee, Planning Manager.  
SD - Taped Hearing.
